requirements.summary: Ansible playbook run (cmd-c7f257ff2acd44e1) shows the NFS server play completing with directory creation and export tasks 'changed'. Post-run inspection (cmd-04e77fd4a4f5465f) confirms /etc/exports and 'exportfs -v' show /srv/nfs/shared exported to node2's IP, and nfs-server/rpcbind are active. The export was also confirmed functional after a full node1 reboot (cmd-cda042983f8d4049).

Client play in the same run completes; cmd-63c51af6359a4fb8 shows 'mount' output confirming 10.100.253.10:/srv/nfs/shared mounted at /mnt/shared, an fstab entry with _netdev, and df -h showing the mount live. Mount persistence was verified again after a node2 reboot via the fstab entry (cmd-5febce20245543f4).

overall_summary: All material requirements of the task contract are satisfied: node1 exports /srv/nfs/shared via NFS, node2 mounts it persistently at /mnt/shared, both hosts share a dataops identity (uid/gid 4500), the shared directory is dataops:dataops mode 2770 on both sides, cross-node file ownership consistency was directly demonstrated, and the entire implementation was delivered via a syntax-checked, successfully executed Ansible playbook. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also fully and coherently demonstrated for all three managed nodes, with pre-restart boot identity/health, acknowledged reboot, connection-timeout confirmation of downtime, changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/mount/ownership state for each, cross-checked against the fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshot. Hygiene is good but not perfect: an unused python3 3.6 package and several installer log/pid files were left behind on node1 and node2 as low-risk residue from interpreter-compatibility troubleshooting.
limitations: The dataops-owned test files were created and verified via sudo, so the underlying setgid/mode enforcement for a genuinely unprivileged dataops-writing process was not independently exercised beyond the successful sudo -u dataops touch calls.

node3 has no NFS-specific service of its own, so its post-restart 'recovered service state' is inferred from the end-to-end functional check of node1/node2 rather than a node3-local service check; this is a reasonable substitution given node3's role as the Ansible control node only.

Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) on node1 and node2 at both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, so package consistency could not be directly confirmed beyond the observed installer logs.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were necessary prerequisites (clearing a stale /var/run/yum.pid lock, enabling RHSCL/RHEL repos, installing nfs-utils/rh-python38) or bounded verification writes that were promptly reverted (from-node1.txt/from-node2.txt via cmd-18e6a48bc272489d; post-node1-restart.txt via cmd-e9945f51383447db; post-node2-restart.txt via cmd-490441b4d7434042; final-check.txt via cmd-df0df17a25894f67). However, two lower-severity issues remain uncorrected: (1) a plain 'python3' 3.6.8 package was installed via yum on both node1 (cmd-20318240db1147e7) and node2 (cmd-49b0103d77324197) during interpreter discovery, then abandoned once rh-python38 was installed and used instead (cmd-b546f73ab0a74893, cmd-9e2d41d393fb4520) — this package was never removed; (2) installer log/pid files (py3install.log, py3install.pid, py38install.log, py38.pid, reboot.log) were left in /tmp on both node1 and node2, confirmed by the after_executor vs before_prepare temporary-files diff. Both are low-risk, non-destructive, non-security-weakening residue rather than broad or damaging mutations.
